lead: Both readings ask what makes a life stand. James says that the one who endures the test will receive the crown of life, and that every good gift, and our very birth by the word of truth, comes from the Father of lights, who never tempts anyone. In Matthew, at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says that it is not calling him “Lord” but doing the will of the Father that matters, and that the wise person builds on the rock of his words. Together they say: trust God’s goodness, and let his word be done in your life.

r.h: Every perfect gift is from above
set: The Letter of James is addressed to Jewish Christians “in the Dispersion” (1:1) and is full of practical teaching, in the spirit of Israel’s wisdom writings. Tradition names its author as James, “the brother of the Lord”, the leader of the church in Jerusalem; some scholars think it was written later by a disciple in his name. The Church receives it as Scripture.

The passage follows verses on trials as occasions for joy and endurance (1:2–4). The Greek peirasmos can mean either a test from outside or an inner temptation; James uses it in both senses and shows how God stands to each.
str: v. 12: a blessing on one who endures; the crown of life.
vv. 13–15: God does not tempt; temptation comes from our own desire, which leads to sin and death.
vv. 16–17: do not be deceived; every good gift is from the Father of lights, who does not change.
v. 18: by his own will God gave us birth by the word of truth, as first fruits of his creation.
kw: The same word for the testing of faith (1:2–3) and for the pull toward sin (1:14). God allows us to be tested, to strengthen us, but he never tempts us to evil.
The crown here is the wreath of the winner or the guest of honour, not of a king. It is eternal life as a gift promised to those who love God (see Revelation 2:10).
The first part of a harvest offered to God. Believers are the first fruits of a new creation that is to follow.
vv: Blessed is anyone who endures temptation. Such a one has stood the test and will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him.
Endurance is not grim effort alone; it is love of God that holds. The crown is promised, and what is promised is given.
No one, when tempted, should say, “I am being tempted by God”; for God cannot be tempted by evil and he himself tempts no one.
A clear word against blaming God for sin. God is wholly good; evil never comes from his will.
Every generous act of giving, with every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.
The sun and stars change and cast shadows; the Father who made them does not. His goodness is the one steady light.
In fulfillment of his own purpose he gave us birth by the word of truth, so that we would become a kind of first fruits of his creatures.
Our new birth is the Father’s gift, by the word of truth. It is first of all his work, and we are called to live it.
ch: The Catechism teaches, with this text, that God is not the author of temptation and that in the Our Father we ask the Father not to let us enter into it, and so to keep us from consenting to evil (CCC 2846–2847). The Church’s teaching on the new birth is that Baptism is a gift of God’s grace, before any merit of ours (CCC 1996–1999, 2008). James’s phrase “the Father of lights” is taken by the Fathers as a name for God as the source of all goodness and light, from whom comes every gift, and the Church’s prayer thanks him for these gifts (in substance).

set: These verses end the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), the first of the five great discourses in Matthew. After the Beatitudes, the teaching on the Law, prayer and trust, Jesus ends with warnings and a parable that call for decision.

The setting is a hill in Galilee. The listeners are the disciples and the crowds (5:1; 7:28). In Palestine a house built on bare sand beside a dry stream bed might stand all summer and be swept away by the first winter flood. A house built on rock remained.
str: v. 21: not saying “Lord, Lord”, but doing the Father’s will, opens the kingdom.
vv. 22–23: many will point to prophecy, exorcism and miracles; Jesus will say, “I never knew you”.
vv. 24–25: the one who hears and acts is like a wise man who built on rock.
vv. 26–27: the one who hears and does not act is like a foolish man who built on sand.
v. 28: the crowds are astounded at his teaching.
kw: Here poieō (“to do”) is the key verb: it occurs again in verses 24 and 26. The Father’s will is not only to be admired but done.
In Hebrew thought to “know” a person is to be in living relationship with him. The tragedy is not a lack of information; the relationship was never real.
A word of amazement. Matthew ends the sermon by saying that Jesus taught “as one having authority” (7:29): his word is not a commentary but a command that creates.
vv: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.
The confession of Jesus as Lord is true and necessary. But it is meant to become a life. Faith that is only on the lips is not yet the faith Jesus asks for.
Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; go away from me, you evildoers.’
The great deeds of the speakers are not denied here; what is missing is the relationship and the doing of the Father’s will. Gifts and signs belong to God, not to us.
“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
Hearing and doing belong together. The rock is Jesus’ own word, received and lived.
The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on rock.
The wise builder is not spared the storm. The house stands because of its foundation.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in teaching on the Our Father: “Thy will be done” is the prayer that we may do the Father’s will, as Jesus did (CCC 2826). It teaches that our works are done by grace: God first gives us the power to will and do the good, and the merit of our works is due to God’s gift (CCC 2008; Philippians 2:13). So the passage does not set faith against works: it describes living faith, which is, as James says, faith that acts (James 2:17). The Church has long read the rock as Christ’s word and, in Christ, the Church founded on him (Matthew 16:18; CCC 552).

qa: If Jesus says that works of power are not enough, is faith in him not enough?

Faith is necessary and is the foundation (CCC 161). But faith that is real shows itself in obedience and love, as the same Lord teaches (John 14:15). Jesus is not saying that works earn heaven by themselves; he is saying that calling him Lord means asking him to rule our lives. The power to do the Father’s will is itself his gift (CCC 2008).
study: James says that God tempts no one and that every good gift comes from the Father of lights. What gift of the past week do I want to thank God for by name?
Jesus says that the wise person hears and acts. What word of Jesus have I heard recently that I have not yet put into practice, and what is one concrete step this week?
